# Results and Discussion

*Assignment 1: Opinion Network Formation — analysis write-up.*
*Generated by `network_analysis.py`; figures in `figures/`.*

### 0. Missing-data policy

Blank cells are treated as **NaN and never imputed**. A respondent who answered nothing is dropped entirely; every respondent who answered at least one item is retained. `"No Comments"` is an explicit choice rather than a non-response, so it maps to the neutral value 3.

This has a direct consequence for how similarity is computed. With NaN present, cosine similarity is undefined, so similarity becomes **pairwise-complete Pearson correlation**: each pair of respondents is correlated over only the items that *both* answered, with each vector centred on that shared subset. On complete rows this is mathematically identical to the mean-centred cosine similarity of Step 2, so the change affects only the incomplete rows — which is the intent.

Of the 96 respondents, 5 were entirely blank and dropped (ids 44, 60, 68, 73, 78), leaving 91. Pairwise overlap is healthy throughout: the minimum number of shared answered items across all 4,095 pairs is **15**, the median is the full **60**, and no pair falls below the `MIN_OVERLAP = 10` floor. Thresholding at $\tau = 0.40$ and removing 3 isolates gives the analysis graph **GA: 88 nodes, 946 edges**.

Four respondents answered only the Technology block (15 of 60 items). They are retained, and their correlations rest on that subset alone, so their ties are noisier than those of complete respondents. Critically, they do **not** cluster together — their degrees are 5, 29, 16 and 6, spread across the network.

### 1. The network is dense, cohesive, and undivided

The network comprises **88 respondents joined by 946 agreement ties**, with a density of **0.247** — roughly one in four of all possible pairs of students hold opinion profiles correlating at $r \geq 0.40$. It forms a **single connected component** with a diameter of **5** and a mean shortest path of **2.01**: any two respondents are separated, on average, by about two intermediate viewpoints.

Clustering is **0.544**, more than twice the **0.253** produced by a random graph of identical size. Agreement is strongly transitive — if two respondents both agree with a third, they usually agree with each other. Combined with short path lengths, this is the signature of a *cohesive* opinion space, not a fragmented one.

Degree assortativity is effectively zero (**+0.037**): respondents with mainstream views show no tendency to agree preferentially with other mainstream respondents. There is no in-group effect.

### 2. There are no opinion factions — the central finding

Louvain returns four communities of sizes 30, 28, 19 and 11, but the partition does not survive scrutiny:

| Evidence | Value | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Modularity $Q$ | **0.148** | Far below the ~0.3 threshold for genuine structure |
| Erdős–Rényi null | $Q = 0.147 \pm 0.006$ ($z = +0.23$) | Indistinguishable from random |
| Configuration-model null | $Q = 0.144 \pm 0.006$ ($z = +0.62$) | Indistinguishable from random, degrees preserved |
| Edges crossing communities | **51.8%** | More ties break the partition than respect it |
| Community count across seeds | 3–5 | The partition is not even stable |

The degree-preserving null is decisive. A configuration-model graph has, by construction, *no* community structure — yet it yields the same modularity as our data. The four communities are an artefact of an algorithm obliged to return a partition whether or not one exists.

The threshold sweep confirms this independently. Modularity climbs from $Q = 0.06$ at $\tau = 0.20$ to $Q = 0.59$ at $\tau = 0.65$, which might appear to vindicate a stricter threshold — but it correlates at **−0.969** with the share of respondents retained. At $\tau = 0.65$ the network looks convincingly factional precisely because it has discarded **53% of the class** and fragmented into 3 components. The apparent communities are a property of the cut, not of the students.

**The class does not divide into opinion camps. It occupies a single broad consensus.**

### 3. The communities differ in intensity, not direction

Profiling the four communities across the survey domains makes this concrete. Every community mean in every domain lies above the neutral midpoint — the full range is **3.73 to 4.50**, and none of the 16 community-by-domain cells falls below 3.0.

| Community | n | Technology | Education | Society | Environment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C0 | 30 | 4.14 | 3.88 | 4.37 | 4.50 |
| C1 | 28 | 3.83 | 4.04 | 4.22 | 4.37 |
| C2 | 19 | 3.91 | 3.95 | 4.25 | 4.39 |
| C3 | 11 | 4.22 | 3.73 | 4.45 | 4.37 |

The largest gap between any two communities in any domain is 0.39 points on a five-point scale. This is why modularity is low: a partition can only be strong if the groups it separates are genuinely different, and at domain level these are not.

Aggregation does conceal some directional splits. On **5 of the 60 individual statements** at least one community falls below the neutral midpoint, so the communities are not merely gradations of assent on every item. These remain too few and too weakly aligned with the partition to generate meaningful modularity.

### 4. Where disagreement exists, it is about technology

Although the class is consensual overall, disagreement is not evenly distributed across topics. Of the **15 most divisive statements, 9 are Technology items**, 5 are Education and 1 is Society. **No Environment item appears at all** — environmental opinion is the most uniform in the survey.

The flashpoints concern automation and AI governance:

| Item | Spread | Class mean |
|---|---|---|
| T07 — robots replacing humans in hazardous work | 1.90 | 4.21 |
| T12 — stricter government regulation of AI | 1.53 | 4.01 |
| E01 — project-based vs examination-oriented learning | 1.52 | 4.32 |
| E02 — written exams accurately measure knowledge | 1.36 | 2.84 |
| E04 — online learning complementing classroom teaching | 1.25 | 3.44 |

By contrast, the strongest consensus items are values rather than policies: continuous lifelong learning (**4.71**), corporate environmental accountability (**4.67**), individual control over personal data (**4.63**), and freedom to express differing opinions (**4.55**). Each has a standard deviation below 0.61.

The class also holds two firmly **negative** positions. It rejects **compulsory class attendance** (E03, mean **2.06** — the strongest single opinion in the survey in either direction) and doubts that **traditional written examinations measure knowledge** (E02, mean 2.84). Both carry high standard deviations (1.12 and 1.11), so they are strongly held rather than unanimous. Together with the endorsement of project-based learning (E01, 4.32), they describe a class sceptical of compulsion and conventional assessment.

The structure of class opinion is therefore: **shared values, contested implementation.** Students agree almost unanimously on ends — sustainability, privacy, openness, lifelong learning — and divide on the technological and institutional means of achieving them.

### 5. Methodological findings

**The missing-data policy changes what the analysis can see.** An earlier version of this pipeline imputed every blank as neutral (3). That silently manufactured structure: the four respondents who answered only the Technology block received 45 identical filler values each, became near-identical to one another, and were grouped by Louvain into a "community" whose members shared nothing but their non-response. Worse, because their item means were pinned at exactly 3.0, they inverted the divisive-item ranking — statements of *strongest consensus* appeared most divisive, since spread was simply measuring distance from neutral. Treating blanks as NaN and correlating on pairwise-complete items removes both effects: the four respondents disperse (degrees 5, 29, 16, 6) and the Technology finding re-emerges.

**The threshold is the analysis.** Because $\tau$ simultaneously determines density, connectivity, and modularity, no structural claim from a thresholded correlation network is interpretable without a sensitivity sweep. Reporting $\tau = 0.40$ alone would have concealed that the community structure at that threshold is indistinguishable from random.

### 6. Limitations

- **Pairwise-complete correlation varies in precision.** Pairs sharing all 60 items yield a more reliable estimate than pairs sharing 15. All pairs are thresholded identically, so ties involving the four sparse respondents carry more uncertainty than the rest.
- **Correlation removes response level.** A respondent agreeing moderately with everything and one agreeing strongly with everything are identical after centring. This is deliberate — it isolates the *pattern* of opinion from acquiescence bias — but the network measures relative, not absolute, agreement.
- **The 60 items are not independent.** Several statements within a domain are near-paraphrases, so effective dimensionality is well below 60 and correlations are inflated. This partly explains the high density.
- **All 1–5 gaps are treated as equal.** Likert data is ordinal; treating "Disagree → Neutral" as the same distance as "Agree → Strongly Agree" is standard but a real simplification.
- **The sample is a single class of 96 students** sharing an academic context, which plausibly explains the consensus directly. The absence of factions may reflect population homogeneity rather than a general property of opinion networks.
- **Edges are undirected and unweighted.** Thresholding discards magnitude: a pair at $r = 0.41$ and a pair at $r = 0.95$ contribute identically.

### 7. Conclusion

The class forms a single, densely connected, highly transitive opinion network with no statistically meaningful community structure. Apparent factions are artefacts of the similarity threshold, and — under a neutral-imputation policy — of missing data. Disagreement is real but narrow: it concentrates in the Technology domain around automation and AI governance, while the strongest consensus attaches to environmental, ethical, and educational values. The appropriate summary is not that the class is divided into camps, but that it is **united on principles and undecided about technology**.
